26772.q: What is Giacometti’s famous figure “Walking Man” doing?
26772.e: Walking Man is a thin figure taking a big step forwards. So he is walking.
26772.m: Walking Man is in the middle of walking.

26773.q: In which city did Alberto Giacometti have his studio for many years?
26773.e: Giacometti worked for a long time in a small studio in Paris. Many of his figures were made there.

26774.e: Tinguely built machines that turn, rattle and squeak. They are works of art that amaze people.
26774.m: Jean Tinguely built moving works of art.

26775.q: What did Jean Tinguely often build his machines from?
26775.e: Tinguely collected old wheels, metal parts and scrap. From these he built his funny machines.
26775.m: Tinguely built machines from scrap metal.

26776.q: In which city is Jean Tinguely’s Carnival Fountain?
26776.e: The Tinguely Fountain has stood in front of the theatre in Basel since 1977. Many metal figures move in the water.
26776.m: The Tinguely Fountain is in Basel.

26777.q: What do the figures in the Tinguely Fountain do?
26777.e: The metal figures in the fountain move and squirt water. That is why lots of people stop to watch them.
26777.m: The figures in the Tinguely Fountain squirt water.

26778.q: In which town was Jean Tinguely born?
26778.e: Tinguely came into the world in Fribourg in 1925. But he moved away as a child.

26779.q: Where is the museum dedicated to Jean Tinguely?
26779.e: The Museum Tinguely stands by the Rhine in Basel. You can see many of his machines moving there.
26779.m: The Museum Tinguely is in Basel.

26780.q: Which artist was Jean Tinguely married to?
26780.e: Niki de Saint Phalle made large, colourful figures. Together with Tinguely she also created joint works of art.
26780.m: Tinguely married Niki de Saint Phalle.

26781.q: What is the big Tinguely machine at the Zürichhorn in Zurich called?
26781.e: Tinguely built the machine “Heureka” for the national exhibition in 1964. Today it stands at the Zürichhorn.
26781.m: The Heureka machine stands in Zurich.

26782.q: Which famous prize did the poet Carl Spitteler win?
26782.e: Carl Spitteler received the Nobel Prize in Literature in 1919. He is still the only winner of this prize born in Switzerland.
26782.m: Carl Spitteler won the Nobel Prize in Literature.

26783.q: What job did Carl Spitteler do?
26783.e: Carl Spitteler was a Swiss poet. He wrote long poems in verse, stories and shorter poems.
26783.m: Carl Spitteler wrote poems as a Swiss poet.

26784.q: Which famous prize did Carl Spitteler receive?
26784.e: Carl Spitteler received the Nobel Prize in Literature for the year 1919. He became the first Swiss-born winner of the literature prize.
26784.m: Spitteler received the Nobel Prize in Literature.

26785.q: Carl Spitteler was born in Liestal. In which canton is Liestal?
26785.e: Liestal is the capital of the canton of Basel-Landschaft. Spitteler came into the world there in 1845.
26785.m: Carl Spitteler came from Liestal in the canton of Basel-Landschaft.

26786.q: In which canton is Liestal, the town where Carl Spitteler was born?
26786.e: Carl Spitteler was born in Liestal in 1845. Liestal is the capital of the canton of Basel-Landschaft.
26786.m: Carl Spitteler came from Liestal in Basel-Landschaft.

26787.q: Who is Spitteler’s long poem “Olympian Spring” about?
26787.e: In “Olympian Spring” Spitteler tells of gods on Mount Olympus. It is his best-known work.

26788.q: What did Carl Spitteler call for in 1914 in his speech “Our Swiss Standpoint”?
26788.e: During the First World War, German-speaking and French-speaking Swiss quarrelled. Spitteler called on them to stick together as Swiss.
26788.m: Spitteler called on the Swiss to stay united.

26789.q: What does Carl Spitteler tell about in his book “Two Little Misogynists”?
26789.e: In this book Spitteler tells of two boys and their quarrels with a girl. In it he remembers his own childhood.
26789.m: Spitteler wrote the childhood story “Two Little Misogynists”.

26790.q: When did the First World War last from and to?
26790.e: The First World War began in 1914 and ended in November 1918. Many countries in Europe fought against each other.
26790.m: The First World War lasted from 1914 to 1918.

26791.q: Did Switzerland fight in the First World War?
26791.e: Switzerland stayed neutral and did not fight alongside any country. But it guarded its borders.
26791.m: Switzerland stayed neutral in the First World War.

26792.q: Who served as General of the Swiss Army in the First World War?
26792.e: Parliament elected Ulrich Wille as General in August 1914. He led the army until the end of the war.
26792.m: Ulrich Wille served as General in the First World War.

26793.q: What did Swiss soldiers mainly do in the First World War?
26793.e: The soldiers stood at the border and made sure no foreign army came into the country. That is why this time is also called the border occupation.
26793.m: In the First World War Swiss soldiers guarded the border.

26794.q: Which aid organisation from Geneva helped prisoners of war in the First World War?
26794.e: The International Committee of the Red Cross searched for missing soldiers and helped prisoners. For this it received the Nobel Peace Prize in 1917.
26794.m: The Red Cross from Geneva helped many prisoners in the First World War.

26795.q: Which illness spread widely in Switzerland too in 1918?
26795.e: Spanish flu was a very dangerous kind of flu. In Switzerland more than 24,000 people died of it.
26795.m: In 1918 Spanish flu raged in Switzerland.

26796.q: What is the big strike in Switzerland in November 1918 called?
26796.e: In the national strike about 250,000 workers stopped work for three days. They wanted better working and living conditions.
26796.m: In November 1918 Switzerland had the national strike.

26797.q: Which country did many people in French-speaking Switzerland support in the First World War?
26797.e: People in western Switzerland speak French and felt close to France. Many German-speaking Swiss, on the other hand, tended to support Germany.
26797.m: In the First World War many French-speaking Swiss supported France.

26798.q: Who had the idea for the “Battle for Cultivation”?
26798.e: The farming expert Friedrich Traugott Wahlen presented his plan in November 1940. That is why it is also called the Wahlen Plan.
26798.m: Friedrich Traugott Wahlen came up with the Battle for Cultivation.

26799.q: What was the aim of the “Battle for Cultivation”?
a: To grow more of its own food
26799.e: During the war Switzerland could only get a little food from abroad. So it had to grow as much as possible itself.
26799.m: The Battle for Cultivation aimed to produce more home-grown food.

26800.q: Where were vegetables even grown during the “Battle for Cultivation”?
a: In parks and on sports grounds
26800.e: Every free piece of land got used. Even city parks, sports grounds and gardens became fields.
26800.m: In the Battle for Cultivation even parks and sports grounds became fields.

26801.q: What was grown in especially large amounts during the “Battle for Cultivation”?
26801.e: Potatoes grow well in Switzerland and fill you up. So a great many potatoes got planted during the war.
26801.m: In the Battle for Cultivation people planted lots of potatoes.

26802.q: Friedrich Traugott Wahlen led the “Battle for Cultivation”. Which office did he hold later?
26802.e: Wahlen got elected to the Federal Council in 1958. He served there from 1959 to 1965.
26802.m: Friedrich Traugott Wahlen later became a Federal Councillor.

26803.q: Why could Switzerland buy only a little food from abroad in the Second World War?
a: Because there was war all around
Because the farmers went on strike
26803.e: The countries around Switzerland were at war. So far fewer goods came across the border.
26803.m: During the war little food came into Switzerland from abroad.

26804.q: Roughly how much of its food could Switzerland produce itself by the end of the Second World War?
26804.e: In 1940 Switzerland produced about half of its food itself. By 1945, thanks to the Battle for Cultivation, it produced about 70 percent.
26804.m: Thanks to the Battle for Cultivation, home-grown food rose to about 70 percent.

26805.q: How does the big monument to General Guisan in Lausanne-Ouchy show the General?
26805.e: In Lausanne-Ouchy there is an equestrian statue. It shows Guisan high up on horseback.
26805.m: Lausanne has an equestrian statue of General Guisan.

26806.q: In which year did General Guisan step down as General?
26806.e: After the end of the war Switzerland no longer needed a General. In August 1945 Guisan said goodbye on the Bundesplatz in Bern.

26807.q: Where did General Guisan gather his officers for the famous briefing in 1940?
26807.e: On 25 July 1940 Guisan called the officers to the meadow on Lake Lucerne. He wanted to give them courage and show the will to defend the country.
26807.m: General Guisan’s famous briefing took place on the Rütli.

26808.q: Where was the army meant to retreat to in case of an attack?
26808.e: In the mountains the army could defend itself better. Many fortresses got built there.
26808.m: In case of attack the army planned to retreat into the Alps.

26809.q: What job did Henri Guisan have alongside the military?
26809.e: Guisan ran the Verte Rive estate in Pully near Lausanne. For a long time the military came on top of his main job.
26809.m: Henri Guisan worked as a farmer.

26810.q: Who elected Henri Guisan as General?
26810.e: In Switzerland the General is elected by Parliament, that is the Federal Assembly. This only happens in wartime or in great danger.
26810.m: The Federal Assembly elects the General.

26811.q: Roughly how many people came to General Guisan’s funeral in 1960?
26811.e: The funeral in Pully was a state funeral. About 300,000 people wanted to say goodbye.
26811.m: About 300,000 people came to General Guisan’s funeral.

26812.q: What is named after General Guisan in many Swiss towns today?
26812.e: Many towns have a Guisanplatz or a Guisanstrasse. That is how people remember the General.
26812.m: Many streets and squares are named after General Guisan.

26813.q: What were ration coupons needed for in the Second World War?
a: To be allowed to buy food
26813.e: Many foods were scarce. With the coupons each person could only buy a certain amount.
26813.m: With ration coupons you could buy a certain amount of food.

26814.q: With ration coupons, did you still have to pay for the food?
a: No, the state paid for everything
26814.e: The coupon only allowed you to buy. You still needed the money for the goods.
26814.m: With ration coupons you still had to pay for the food.

26815.q: What does it mean when a food is “rationed”?
a: Everyone gets only a set amount
26815.e: With rationing, whatever is scarce gets shared out fairly. Each person gets a fixed share.
26815.m: Rationed means that everyone gets only a set amount.

26816.q: Until when did Switzerland still have rationing after the Second World War?
26816.e: After the end of the war, rationing got lifted step by step. By July 1948 it had ended completely.

26817.q: From which year in the Second World War was bread rationed too?
26817.e: In October 1942 bread also went on the ration card. Other goods such as sugar had been rationed earlier.
26817.m: From 1942 bread in Switzerland was rationed too.

26818.q: How was bread sold from 1940 so that people would eat less of it?
26818.e: From July 1940 bread could no longer be sold fresh. You eat old bread more slowly and eat less of it.
26818.m: From 1940 bread could no longer be sold fresh.

26819.q: Did Switzerland already have ration cards in the First World War?
26819.e: From 1917 rice, sugar and then bread and flour were rationed. Later butter, cheese and milk were added.
26819.m: Even in the First World War there were ration cards for bread.

26820.q: Who got bigger portions from 1942 in the Second World War?
26820.e: Anyone doing hard physical work needed more strength. So heavy labourers got more food.

26821.q: In which city did the Landi 1939 take place?
26821.e: The Landi lay on both shores of Lake Zurich. One part sat in Wollishofen, the other at the Zürichhorn.
26821.m: The Landi 1939 took place in Zurich.

26822.q: What kind of transport carried people high over Lake Zurich at the Landi?
26822.e: The cable car linked the two shores between two towers 75 metres high. It became the landmark of the Landi.
26822.m: At the Landi 1939 a cable car floated over Lake Zurich.

26823.q: What was the water channel called where you rode small boats at the Landi?
26823.e: Small boats with six seats travelled through the exhibition on the Schifflibach. One ride cost 50 rappen.
26823.m: On the Schifflibach you rode boats through the Landi.

26824.q: Roughly how many admissions did the Landi 1939 have?
26824.e: The Landi counted over ten and a half million paid admissions. That is more than twice as many as Switzerland’s population at the time.
26824.m: The Landi had over 10 million admissions.

26825.q: What hung above the Höhenstrasse at the Landi?
26825.e: Above the Höhenstrasse hung the flags of about 3,000 municipalities and of all the cantons. This showed how varied Switzerland is.
26825.m: The flags of the municipalities hung above the Landi’s Höhenstrasse.

26826.q: Which event began in 1939 while the Landi was still open?
26826.e: The Landi stayed open from May to October 1939. On 1 September 1939 Germany invaded Poland.
26826.m: The Second World War began during the Landi 1939.

26827.q: Roughly how long was the Landi 1939 open?
26827.e: The Landi opened on 6 May 1939 and lasted until the end of October.
26827.m: The Landi 1939 lasted about half a year.

26828.q: What was the Landi 1939 mainly meant to show people?
26828.e: At a time full of danger of war, the Landi wanted to strengthen unity. It showed what makes Switzerland special.
26828.m: The Landi showed what makes Switzerland Swiss.

26829.q: Since which year has the AHV (old-age insurance) existed?
26829.e: The AHV came into force on 1 January 1948. Since then older people have received a pension.

26830.q: What is the money you get from the AHV every month called?
26830.e: The AHV pays out a pension every month. The pension helps people live after they stop working.
26830.m: The money from the AHV is called a pension.

26831.q: Who mainly gets money from the AHV?
26831.e: Anyone who has reached retirement age gets money from the AHV. That way older people also have an income.
26831.m: The AHV mainly pays money to older people.

26832.q: Who else gets money from the AHV if their father or mother dies?
26832.e: The H in AHV stands for survivors. Children who lose a parent get an orphan’s pension.
26832.m: The AHV also helps children whose father or mother has died.

26833.q: How did the people vote on the AHV in 1947?
26833.e: On 6 July 1947 about 80 percent of voters said yes. That is a very large majority.
26833.m: In 1947 the people said a very clear yes to the AHV.

26834.q: From what age do men normally get the AHV pension (as of 2026)?
26834.e: The normal retirement age for men is 65. For women it is being raised step by step to 65 as well by 2028.
26834.m: Men normally get the AHV pension from age 65.

26835.q: Who pays money into the AHV?
26835.e: A small part of every wage goes to the AHV. The employer pays the same amount on top.
26835.m: Workers and employers pay into the AHV together.

26836.q: Roughly how long did Expo 64 last?
26836.e: The exhibition stayed open from 30 April to 25 October 1964. That is almost six months.

26837.q: What kind of vehicle was the “Mésoscaphe” at Expo 64?
26837.e: The Mésoscaphe served as a submarine for visitors. With it you could travel under water.
26837.m: The Mésoscaphe at Expo 64 travelled under water as a submarine.

26838.e: Jacques Piccard became a famous deep-sea explorer. His father Auguste Piccard flew a balloon into the stratosphere.

26839.q: Where can you see the Mésoscaphe today?
a: At the Swiss Museum of Transport in Lucerne
26839.e: Today the boat belongs to the Swiss Museum of Transport in Lucerne. It is on display there.
26839.m: You can see the Mésoscaphe today at the Swiss Museum of Transport in Lucerne.

26840.q: What do you call a train that runs on just one rail, like the one at Expo 64?
26840.e: “Mono” means “one” and “rail” is the track. The monorail became one of the big attractions of the Expo.
26840.m: A monorail runs on just one rail.

26841.q: Which artist built the machine “Heureka” for Expo 64?
26841.e: Jean Tinguely loved building works of art that move. His machine “Heureka” drew many visitors.

26842.q: In which city does the machine “Heureka” stand today?
26842.e: After the Expo, “Heureka” went to the Zürichhorn. It still stands there by the lake shore today.
26842.m: The machine “Heureka” stands in Zurich today.

26843.q: In which city did the national exhibition Expo 64 take place?
26843.e: Expo 64 took place in 1964 in Lausanne on Lake Geneva. The national exhibition before it, the Landi 1939, took place in Zurich.

26845.q: Who could vote in the national referendum on women’s right to vote?
26845.e: Women did not yet have the right to vote. So the men had to decide about it.
26845.m: Only men voted on women’s right to vote.

26846.q: In which year could women finally vote in the last canton too?
26846.e: In 1990 the Federal Supreme Court decided that women may have their say everywhere. From then on all Swiss women had the right to vote.
26846.m: Since 1990 women can vote in all cantons.

26847.q: Who became the first woman President of the Swiss Confederation?
26847.e: Ruth Dreifuss served as President in 1999. She became the first woman in this office.
26847.m: Ruth Dreifuss became the first woman President of Switzerland.

26848.q: Who became the first woman Federal Councillor in Switzerland?
26848.e: Elisabeth Kopp got elected to the Federal Council in 1984 as the first woman. She came from the canton of Zurich.
26848.m: Elisabeth Kopp became the first woman Federal Councillor.

26849.q: What can you do with the right to vote?
26849.e: With the right to vote you can say yes or no in referendums. You can also elect politicians.
26849.m: With the right to vote you can vote and elect people.

26850.q: Since which year has the canton of Jura existed?
26850.e: The canton of Jura came into being on 1 January 1979. It is the youngest canton in Switzerland.
26850.m: The canton of Jura has existed since 1979.

26851.q: Which canton did the area of the canton of Jura belong to before?
26851.e: The northern Jura belonged to the canton of Bern for a long time. But many people there wanted their own canton.
26851.m: The canton of Jura used to belong to the canton of Bern.

26852.q: What is the capital of the canton of Jura?
26852.e: The government and the parliament of the canton sit there.
26852.m: Delémont is the capital of the canton of Jura.

26853.q: Which language do people mainly speak in the canton of Jura?
26853.e: Almost everyone in the Jura speaks French. Only one municipality is German-speaking.
26853.m: In the canton of Jura people mainly speak French.

26854.q: Which neighbouring country borders the canton of Jura?
26854.e: The canton of Jura lies in the north-west of Switzerland. To the north and west it borders France.
26854.m: The canton of Jura borders France.

26855.q: Which town moved from the canton of Bern to the canton of Jura in 2026?
26855.e: The voters of Moutier said yes to the move in 2021. Since 1 January 2026 the town has belonged to the canton of Jura.
26855.m: Moutier has belonged to the canton of Jura since 2026.

26856.q: How many voters across Switzerland said yes to the new canton of Jura in 1978?
26856.e: On 24 September 1978, 82 percent agreed. All the cantons said yes as well.
26856.m: In 1978 over 80 percent said yes to the canton of Jura.

26857.q: Which letters are on number plates from the canton of Jura?
26857.e: Every canton has a two-letter code. For Jura it is the first two letters of the name.
26857.m: The code for the canton of Jura is JU.

26858.q: Which university built the solar wind sail for the Moon?
26858.e: Researchers at the Physics Institute in Bern planned the experiment. It became the only non-American experiment on the first Moon landing.
26858.m: The solar wind sail came from the University of Bern.

26859.q: On which Moon mission did the solar wind sail first go to the Moon?
26859.e: It flew on the mission of the first Moon landing. After that the sail went on further Moon flights too.
26859.m: The solar wind sail flew to the Moon with Apollo 11.

26860.q: In which year did the solar wind sail first stand on the Moon?
26860.e: In July 1969 people landed on the Moon for the first time. They brought the sail from Bern with them.
26860.m: In 1969 the solar wind sail stood on the Moon for the first time.

26861.q: Which astronaut set up the solar wind sail on the Moon?
26861.e: Buzz Aldrin pushed the sail into the Moon’s ground. He became the second person on the Moon.
26861.m: Buzz Aldrin set up the solar wind sail.

26862.q: When was the solar wind sail set up during the first Moon landing?
26862.e: The sail had to collect particles for as long as possible. So it went up even before the American flag.
26862.m: The solar wind sail stood on the Moon even before the US flag.

26863.q: What material was the solar wind sail made of?
26863.e: The sail consisted of a thin aluminium foil. The whole device weighed only about 430 grams.
26863.m: The solar wind sail consisted of aluminium foil.

26864.q: What did the solar wind sail catch on the Moon?
26864.e: Tiny particles constantly fly from the Sun into space. On the Moon they got stuck in the foil.
26864.m: The solar wind sail caught tiny particles from the Sun.

26865.q: What happened to the foil of the solar wind sail after the experiment?
26865.e: The astronauts took the foil back with them. In Bern the particles got measured precisely in the laboratory.
26865.m: The foil of the solar wind sail got examined on Earth.

26867.q: Who had to agree to Switzerland joining the UN?
26867.e: There was a referendum on joining. It needed a majority of voters and of the cantons.
26867.m: The people and the cantons agreed to joining the UN.

26868.q: Did Switzerland have to give up its neutrality to join the UN?
26868.e: Switzerland joined the UN as a neutral country. It said so clearly in its application.
26868.m: Even as a UN member, Switzerland is neutral.

26869.q: In which Swiss city does the UN have a large headquarters?
26869.e: Many people work for the UN in the Palais des Nations. It is its most important seat in Europe.
26869.m: The UN has a large headquarters in Geneva.

26870.q: What does the abbreviation UN stand for?
26870.e: UN is short for “United Nations”. Its full name is the United Nations Organization.

26871.q: Which important UN body did Switzerland sit on in 2023 and 2024?
26871.e: The Security Council looks after peace in the world. Switzerland became a member for two years for the first time.
26871.m: Switzerland sat on the UN Security Council in 2023 and 2024.

26872.q: What is the UN palace in Geneva called?
26872.e: The palace stands in a large park on Lake Geneva. The flags of many countries fly in front of the building.
26872.m: The UN palace in Geneva is called the Palais des Nations.

26873.q: How many voters said yes to joining the UN in 2002?
26873.e: About 55 percent of voters said yes. Among the cantons it was also very close.
26873.m: Slightly more than half said yes to joining the UN.

26874.q: In which year did Swiss television start trial broadcasts?
26874.e: Trial broadcasting started in July 1953. There was about an hour of programmes on five evenings a week.
26874.m: Swiss television started trial broadcasts in 1953.

26875.q: In which city was Switzerland’s first television studio?
26875.e: The first studio had the name Studio Bellerive. It stood in the Seefeld district.
26875.m: Switzerland’s first television studio stood in Zurich.

26876.q: What did the first television pictures in Switzerland look like?
26876.e: The first televisions only showed shades of grey. Colour only came many years later.
26876.m: The first television pictures came in black and white.

26877.q: From which year did Switzerland have colour television?
26877.e: Colour television began on 1 October 1968. A colour television cost about 3,000 francs at that time.
26877.m: Switzerland has had colour television since 1968.

26878.q: At the start, how long did the television programme in Switzerland last each evening?
26878.e: At first there was only a short evening programme. After that the screen went blank again.
26878.m: At first there was only about one hour of television each evening.

26879.q: Which news programme did Swiss television already have during the trial period?
26879.e: The Tagesschau is the oldest news programme on Swiss television. It is still on every evening today.
26879.m: The Tagesschau is the oldest news programme on Swiss television.

26880.q: From which year were there adverts on Swiss television?
26880.e: The first advert went out on 1 February 1965. At first adverts were limited to a few minutes a day.
26880.m: Swiss television has had adverts since 1965.

26881.q: Where were many of the very first televisions in Switzerland?
26881.e: At first only about 920 people had a television licence. Most of them ran restaurants or inns, and the guests watched together.
26881.m: Many of the first televisions stood in restaurants.

26882.q: In which year was Swissair founded?
26882.e: Swissair came into being in 1931 from two smaller airlines. They had the names Ad Astra Aero and Balair.

26883.q: What role did Nelly Diener have at Swissair in 1934?
26883.e: Nelly Diener looked after the passengers on board. She became the first woman in Europe with this job.
26883.m: Nelly Diener became Europe’s first flight attendant.

26884.q: To which airport did Swissair move in 1948?
26884.e: Before that Swissair flew from Dübendorf airfield. In 1948 it moved to the new airport in Kloten.
26884.m: From 1948 Swissair flew from Zurich-Kloten airport.

26885.q: What is the 2001 event called when all Swissair planes had to stay on the ground?
26885.e: Swissair had no money left, for example to pay for fuel. So on 2 October 2001 all its planes stood still.

26886.e: The new airline Swiss grew out of the company Crossair. It took over many of Swissair’s planes and routes.
26886.m: Swissair got followed by the airline Swiss.

26887.q: Which symbol was on the tail of Swissair planes?
26887.e: A white cross shone out on the red tail. That way you recognised planes from Switzerland straight away.
26887.m: The Swiss cross appeared on the tail of Swissair planes.

26888.q: From which year did Swissair fly jet planes?
26888.e: In 1960 the first Swissair jets flew to London and New York. They were much faster than propeller planes.

26889.q: What do people often light on hills and mountains on 1 August?
26889.e: On the evening of 1 August big bonfires burn on many hills and mountains. You can see them from far away.
26889.m: On 1 August bonfires shine on the mountains.

26890.q: What do children often carry through the village on the evening of 1 August?
26890.e: Many children go for a walk in the evening with lanterns. The lanterns often have a Swiss cross or cantonal coats of arms on them.
26890.m: On 1 August children carry colourful lanterns.

26891.q: Which bread roll with a cross cut into it do people eat on 1 August?
26891.e: The 1 August roll has a cross cut into it and often a small Swiss flag. It is sold around the National Day.
26891.m: On 1 August people like to eat a roll with a cross.

26892.q: Who gives a speech to the whole of Switzerland on 1 August?
a: The captain of the national football team
26892.e: The President of the Confederation gives a speech for the National Day. It is broadcast on radio and television.
26892.m: On 1 August the President speaks to Switzerland.

26893.q: What is the Swiss national anthem called?
26893.e: The Swiss national anthem is called the Swiss Psalm. People sing it on 1 August, for example.
26893.m: Our national anthem is called the Swiss Psalm.

26894.q: How does the German text of the Swiss Psalm begin?
26894.e: The Swiss Psalm begins with the words “Trittst im Morgenrot daher” (When you come in the red of morning). The anthem describes sun, mountains and nature.
26894.m: The Swiss Psalm begins with “Trittst im Morgenrot daher”.

26895.q: Who wrote the tune of the Swiss Psalm?
26895.e: The tune comes from Alberik Zwyssig, a monk from Wettingen Abbey. He wrote it in 1841.
26895.m: The monk Alberik Zwyssig composed the Swiss Psalm.

26896.q: With which words does the Swiss Psalm begin?
a: Heidi, your world is the mountains
26896.e: The Swiss Psalm begins with “Trittst im Morgenrot daher”. Leonhard Widmer wrote the words and Alberik Zwyssig the tune.
26896.m: The Swiss Psalm begins with “Trittst im Morgenrot daher”.

26897.q: Since which year has the Swiss Psalm finally been the official national anthem?
26897.e: In 1961 the Federal Council first made the Swiss Psalm the anthem on a trial basis. Since 1981 it has been the official national anthem for good.
26897.m: Since 1981 the Swiss Psalm has officially been our anthem.

26898.q: On which occasion do you often hear the Swiss Psalm on television?
a: When a Swiss national team plays
26898.e: The Swiss Psalm is played before international matches of the Swiss national team. You also hear it at medal ceremonies.
26898.m: The Swiss Psalm is played before international matches.

26899.q: Which earlier song served as the anthem for a long time before the Swiss Psalm?
26899.e: People used to sing “Rufst du, mein Vaterland”. It had the same tune as the British royal anthem, so it got replaced.
26899.m: “Rufst du, mein Vaterland” used to be the Swiss anthem.

26900.q: Which national language do most people in Switzerland speak?
26900.e: About six in ten people in Switzerland mainly speak German. In everyday life they usually speak Swiss German.
26900.m: German is the most widely spoken national language in Switzerland.

26901.q: In which canton do people speak Romansh?
26901.e: Romansh is spoken in the canton of Grisons, for example in the Engadine. It is the smallest of the four national languages.
26901.m: Romansh is at home in the canton of Grisons.

26902.q: Which language do people speak in the canton of Ticino?
26902.e: In Ticino, south of the Alps, people speak Italian. Some valleys in the Grisons are Italian-speaking too.

26903.q: Which word do people use as a greeting in Romansh?
26903.e: “Allegra” is a well-known greeting in Romansh. It means something like “Be glad”.
26903.m: In Romansh you say “Allegra” as a greeting.

26904.q: Which country has the letters CH on its cars?
26904.e: CH is short for the Latin name of Switzerland: Confoederatio Helvetica.

26905.q: Which canton has three official languages?
26905.e: In the canton of Grisons, German, Romansh and Italian are official languages. It is the only trilingual canton.
26905.m: The Grisons is the only trilingual canton.

26906.e: Helvetia is a female figure who represents Switzerland. She is also called the mother of the nation.
26906.m: Helvetia is the female figure who stands for Switzerland.

26907.q: What does Helvetia hold in her hands on the 2-franc coin?
26907.e: On the 2-franc coin Helvetia stands with a spear. With her other hand she holds a shield with the Swiss cross.
26907.m: Helvetia carries a spear and a shield.

26908.q: What is shown on Helvetia’s shield?
26908.e: On Helvetia’s shield you can see the Swiss cross. It shows that she stands for Switzerland.
26908.m: Helvetia’s shield shows the Swiss cross.

26909.q: On which Swiss coins can you see the standing Helvetia?
26909.e: The standing Helvetia is on the 1-franc coin, the 2-franc coin and the half-franc coin. The 5-franc coin shows a herdsman’s head.
26909.m: The standing Helvetia is on the 1-franc and 2-franc coins.

26910.q: Which ancient people does Helvetia get her name from?
26910.e: The Helvetii were a Celtic people in the area of today’s Switzerland. The name Helvetia comes from them.
26910.m: Helvetia is named after the Celtic Helvetii.

26911.q: Where does Helvetia sit in a well-known statue in Basel?
a: On the bank of the Rhine
On a ship in the harbour
26911.e: On the Kleinbasel bank of the Rhine near the Middle Bridge sits the statue “Helvetia on her Travels”. She looks at the Rhine, with her shield and spear beside her.
26911.m: In Basel Helvetia sits on the bank of the Rhine near the Middle Bridge.

a: Cows go up to the alpine pasture
26912.e: At the Alpaufzug farmers take their cows up to the alpine pasture. There the animals eat fresh mountain grass all summer.
26912.m: At the Alpaufzug the cows go up to the alpine pasture.

26913.q: In which season does the Alpaufzug usually take place?
26913.e: The Alpaufzug is usually in June, when enough grass grows on the alpine pastures. Then the alpine summer begins.
26913.m: In early summer the cows go up to the alpine pasture.

26914.q: What do cows often wear round their necks at the Alpaufzug?
26914.e: At the Alpaufzug the cows often wear big bells. The loud ringing is part of the celebration.
26914.m: Big cowbells ring at the Alpaufzug.

26915.q: What is the celebration called when the cows come back down from the alpine pasture in autumn?
26915.e: In September the cows return to the valley. This celebration is called the Alpabzug or Alpabfahrt, in French Désalpe.
26915.m: At the Alpabzug the cows come down to the valley in autumn.

26916.q: What does the alpine dairyman make from the milk up on the pasture?
26916.e: The dairyman turns the milk into alpine cheese up on the pasture. This cheese is brought down to the valley in autumn.
26916.m: On the alpine pasture the dairyman makes cheese from milk.

26917.q: What are the cows decorated with at the Alpabzug?
26917.e: At the Alpabzug the cows often wear flower decorations on their heads. This shows that the alpine summer went well.
26917.m: At the Alpabzug the cows wear flower decorations.

26918.q: What is the house on the alpine pasture called where the dairyman lives and makes cheese?
26918.e: Up on the pasture the dairyman lives in an alpine hut. The big cauldron in which he makes cheese is there too.
26918.m: On the alpine pasture the dairyman lives in an alpine hut.

26919.q: In which city do people celebrate Sechseläuten?
26919.e: Sechseläuten is a spring festival in Zurich. It is celebrated by the city’s guilds.
26919.m: Sechseläuten is a spring festival in Zurich.

26920.q: What is the snowman called that is burned at Sechseläuten?
26920.e: The Böögg is a big snowman made of cotton wool. He stands on a pile of wood and is set alight.
26920.m: The Böögg is the snowman at Sechseläuten.

26921.q: What does the Böögg stand for?
26921.e: The Böögg is a symbol of winter. When he burns, winter is chased away.

26922.q: What is it supposed to mean when the Böögg’s head explodes very quickly?
26922.e: The Böögg’s head is filled with firecrackers. People say the faster the head explodes, the lovelier the summer will be.
26922.m: If the Böögg explodes quickly, there is supposed to be a lovely summer.

26923.q: At what time is the Böögg set alight?
26923.e: The pile of wood is lit at six o’clock in the evening. That is where the name Sechseläuten (six o’clock ringing) comes from.
26923.m: The Böögg is set alight at six o’clock in the evening.

26924.q: In which month does Sechseläuten usually take place?
26924.e: Sechseläuten is usually on the third Monday in April. It celebrates spring.
26924.m: Sechseläuten usually takes place in April.

26925.q: Who rides round the fire with the Böögg at Sechseläuten?
26925.e: The members of the Zurich guilds ride on horses round the burning pile of wood. They wear old costumes as they do so.
26925.m: At Sechseläuten the guild members ride round the fire.

26926.q: What is the square in Zurich called where the Böögg burns?
26926.e: The Böögg burns on the Sechseläutenplatz near Bellevue. The square is close to Lake Zurich.
26926.m: The Böögg burns on the Sechseläutenplatz.

26927.q: What is the start of Basel Carnival early in the morning called?
26927.e: Basel Carnival begins with the Morgestraich. At 4 in the morning all the lights in the old town go out and the carnival groups set off.
26927.m: Basel Carnival begins with the Morgestraich.

26928.q: At what time does the Morgestraich begin?
26928.e: The Morgestraich begins on Monday at 4 in the morning. It is still dark then and only the lanterns shine.
26928.m: The Morgestraich begins at 4 in the morning.

26929.q: How long does Basel Carnival last?
26929.e: Basel Carnival lasts exactly 72 hours, so three days. People in Basel call it “the three loveliest days”.

26930.q: Which instruments do the carnival groups mainly play at Basel Carnival?
26930.e: Piccolos, which are small flutes, and drums are typical of Basel Carnival. The groups march through the lanes playing.
26930.m: At Basel Carnival people play piccolos and drums.

26931.q: What are the face masks at Basel Carnival called?
26931.e: The masks at Basel Carnival are called Larven. They are often big and brightly painted.
26931.m: The masks at Basel Carnival are called Larven.

26932.q: What do people in Basel call confetti?
26932.e: In Basel people call confetti “Räppli”. At carnival time it lies everywhere on the streets.
26932.m: In Basel confetti is called Räppli.

26933.q: Which character with a big nose and yellow hair belongs to Basel Carnival?
26933.e: The Waggis is a typical character of Basel Carnival. He has a big nose and wild yellow hair and likes to hand out Räppli.
26933.m: The Waggis is a well-known character of Basel Carnival.

26934.q: What do the carnival groups carry on their heads or on poles at the Morgestraich?
26934.e: At the Morgestraich the carnival people carry painted lanterns. They glow in the dark city.
26934.m: Painted lanterns glow at the Morgestraich.

26935.q: In which town does the Fête des Vignerons take place?
26935.e: The Fête des Vignerons takes place in Vevey on Lake Geneva. The town is in the canton of Vaud.
26935.m: The Fête des Vignerons takes place in Vevey.

26936.q: Who does the Fête des Vignerons celebrate?
26936.e: The word “vignerons” means winegrowers. The festival honours their work in the vineyards.
26936.m: The Fête des Vignerons celebrates the winegrowers.

26937.q: Roughly how often does the Fête des Vignerons take place?
a: About four times every hundred years
26937.e: The Fête des Vignerons is very rare. It only takes place about every 20 to 25 years, so four or five times a century.
26937.m: The Fête des Vignerons happens only a few times a century.

26938.q: In which year did the last Fête des Vignerons take place (as of 2026)?
26938.e: The last Fête des Vignerons took place in summer 2019. The one before took place in 1999.
26938.m: The last Fête des Vignerons took place in 2019.

26939.e: Vevey lies on the shore of Lake Geneva. The vineyards of Lavaux are nearby.

26940.q: Which plant is at the centre of the Fête des Vignerons?
26940.e: Winegrowers plant grapevines and harvest grapes. That is what the whole festival is about.
26940.m: At the Fête des Vignerons everything revolves around the grapevine.

26941.q: Which important list has the Fête des Vignerons been on since 2016?
a: The list of the Wonders of the World
26941.e: In 2016 UNESCO added the Fête des Vignerons to the list of the Intangible Cultural Heritage of Humanity. It became the first Swiss tradition on this list.
26941.m: The Fête des Vignerons is part of UNESCO’s cultural heritage.

26942.q: On which day do people in the Grisons celebrate Chalandamarz?
26942.e: Chalandamarz is celebrated on 1 March. The name comes from the Latin word for the first day of March.

26943.q: What do the children want to drive away with their bells at Chalandamarz?
26943.e: The children go through the village with loud bells. This is meant to drive winter away.
26943.m: At Chalandamarz children ring winter away.

26944.q: Who goes through the village with bells at Chalandamarz?
26944.e: At Chalandamarz it is mainly schoolchildren who are out and about. They sing songs and ring bells.
26944.m: At Chalandamarz schoolchildren go round with bells.

26945.q: What is the famous children’s book about a boy at Chalandamarz called?
26945.e: The book “A Bell for Ursli” tells of Ursli, who wants a big bell for Chalandamarz. It came out in 1945.
26945.m: “A Bell for Ursli” tells of Chalandamarz.

26946.q: Which bell does Ursli really want in the book “A Bell for Ursli”?
26946.e: At first Ursli only gets a small bell. So he fetches the biggest bell from the Maiensäss, his family’s summer hut in the mountains.
26946.m: Ursli wants to carry the biggest bell at Chalandamarz.

26947.q: In which language do the children often sing at Chalandamarz?
26947.e: Chalandamarz is especially well known in the Engadine. There the children sing many songs in Romansh.
26947.m: At Chalandamarz children often sing Romansh songs.

26948.q: Who painted the pictures for the book “A Bell for Ursli”?
26948.e: Alois Carigiet painted the pictures in “A Bell for Ursli”. The words come from another author, a woman from the Engadine.
26948.m: Alois Carigiet painted the pictures for “A Bell for Ursli”.

26949.e: Schwingen is a Swiss form of wrestling. Two wrestlers each try to throw the other onto his back.

26950.q: What do the Schwingen wrestlers fight on?
26950.e: The wrestlers fight in a round ring filled with sawdust. The soft sawdust protects them when they fall.

26951.q: What does a Schwingen wrestler wear over his clothes?
26951.e: Over his clothes a wrestler wears short breeches made of strong cloth. His opponent grabs hold of these breeches.
26951.m: Schwingen wrestlers wear short breeches made of strong cloth.

26952.q: When has a Schwingen wrestler won?
a: When the opponent lies on his back
When he reaches the finish first
26952.e: A wrestler wins when he gets both of his opponent’s shoulder blades onto the ground. Then the bout is decided.
26952.m: Whoever puts the opponent on his back wins the bout.

26953.q: What does the winner of a Schwingen bout often do for the loser?
a: He brushes the sawdust off his back
26953.e: After the fight the winner brushes the sawdust off the loser’s back. It is a sign of respect.
26953.m: The winner brushes the sawdust off the loser.

26954.q: Which animal does the winner of the Federal Wrestling Festival get as a prize?
26954.e: The wrestling king gets the winner’s Muni, a young bull. “Muni” is the Swiss word for bull.
26954.m: The wrestling king wins a Muni.

26955.q: What is the winner of the Federal Wrestling Festival called?
26955.e: Whoever wins the Federal Wrestling and Alpine Festival is the wrestling king. That is the highest title in Schwingen.
26955.m: The winner of the Federal Festival is called the wrestling king.

26956.q: How often does the Federal Wrestling and Alpine Festival take place?
26956.e: The Federal Wrestling and Alpine Festival takes place every three years. It is one of the biggest sporting events in Switzerland.
26956.m: The Federal Wrestling Festival takes place every three years.

26957.q: What does the Hornuss look like, which players hit a long way in Hornussen?
26957.e: The Hornuss is a small, flat disc. It flies very fast and far through the air.
26957.m: In Hornussen you hit the Hornuss.

26958.q: What do players use to stop the Hornuss in Hornussen?
26958.e: The fielders throw their Schindel, a wooden board on a handle, into the air. That is how they try to stop the Hornuss.
26958.m: In Hornussen you stop the Hornuss with wooden boards.

26959.q: The name Hornuss sounds like the German word for hornet. Why is it called that?
a: It buzzes like a hornet as it flies
26959.e: The Hornuss makes a buzzing sound as it flies fast. It sounds like a hornet.
26959.m: The Hornuss buzzes like a hornet as it flies.

26960.q: What do you hit the Hornuss with in Hornussen?
26960.e: The bat in Hornussen is a long, bendy stick with a block of wood at the end. The batter swings it in an arc and hits the Hornuss.
26960.m: You hit the Hornuss with a long, bendy stick.

26961.q: Where do people mainly play Hornussen?
26961.e: Hornussen needs lots of space because the Hornuss flies a long way. So it is played on big meadows.
26961.m: Hornussen is played on a big meadow.

26962.q: Which part of Switzerland does Hornussen especially come from?
a: From the Emmental and the Bern area
26962.e: Hornussen is especially popular in the canton of Bern, for example in the Emmental. It is also called a farmers’ sport.
26962.m: Hornussen is mainly played in the canton of Bern.

26963.q: How many teams play against each other in a game of Hornussen?
26963.e: In Hornussen two teams compete against each other. One bats while the other stands in the field and stops the Hornuss, then they swap.
26963.m: In Hornussen two teams play against each other.

26964.q: What material is an alphorn made of?
26964.e: An alphorn is made of wood, usually spruce. It is hollow inside.
26964.m: An alphorn is made of wood.

26965.q: Roughly how long is an alphorn?
26965.e: An alphorn is usually about 3 to 4 metres long. At the bottom end it curves upwards.
26965.m: An alphorn is about 3 to 4 metres long.

26966.q: How do you play the alphorn?
26966.e: With the alphorn you blow into the mouthpiece with your lips. Different notes come from how tight your lips are.
26966.m: You blow into the alphorn with your lips.

26967.q: What did herdsmen use the alphorn for in the past?
26967.e: In the past herdsmen used the alphorn to send each other signals over long distances. You could hear it far across the mountains.
26967.m: Herdsmen sent each other signals with the alphorn.

26968.q: What does an alphorn not have?
26968.e: The alphorn has no finger holes, keys or valves. The notes come only from the player’s lips.
26968.m: An alphorn has no finger holes and keys.

26969.q: Where does the bottom end of the alphorn rest while you play?
26969.e: Because the alphorn is so long, the curved end stands on the ground while you play. The player stands upright behind it.
26969.m: While you play, the alphorn rests on the ground.

26970.q: Which music do you often hear together with the alphorn at folk festivals?
26970.e: At Swiss folk festivals alphorn players and yodellers often perform together. Both are part of folk music.
26970.m: Alphorn and yodelling are part of Swiss folk music.

26971.q: Where does the Unspunnen Festival take place?
26971.e: The Unspunnen Festival takes place in Interlaken in the Bernese Oberland. It is named after the ruined Unspunnen Castle.
26971.m: The Unspunnen Festival is in Interlaken.

26972.q: What is thrown as far as possible at the Unspunnen Festival?
26972.e: In stone throwing, strong men throw the Unspunnen Stone as far as they can. It is the best-known contest at the festival.
26972.m: At the Unspunnen Festival people throw a heavy stone.

26973.q: Roughly how heavy is the Unspunnen Stone?
26973.e: The Unspunnen Stone originally weighed 83.5 kilograms. Only very strong men can throw it far.
26973.m: The Unspunnen Stone weighs about 83 kilograms.

26974.q: In which year did the first Unspunnen Festival take place?
26974.e: The first Unspunnen Festival took place in 1805. It was meant to bring town and country closer together again.
26974.m: The first Unspunnen Festival took place in 1805.

26975.q: What do many visitors and performers wear at the Unspunnen Festival?
26975.e: At the Unspunnen Festival costume groups from all over Switzerland show their beautiful traditional costumes. It is also a big costume festival.
26975.m: At the Unspunnen Festival people wear beautiful traditional costumes.

26976.q: Roughly how often does the Unspunnen Festival take place today?
26976.e: The Unspunnen Festival does not take place every year. Today it is held about every twelve years, most recently in 2017.
26976.m: The Unspunnen Festival takes place about every twelve years.

26977.q: What has happened to the Unspunnen Stone more than once?
26977.e: The Unspunnen Stone got stolen in 1984 and 2005. After the first theft it came back in 2001; since 2005 it has been missing, so today people throw a copy.
26977.m: The Unspunnen Stone has been stolen twice.

26978.q: In which city does the Zibelemärit take place?
26978.e: The Zibelemärit is a famous market in the city of Bern. It takes place on squares and in lanes of the old town.
26978.m: The Zibelemärit takes place in Bern.

26979.q: What is mainly sold at the Zibelemärit?
26979.e: “Zibele” is the Bernese German word for onions. At the market there are tonnes of onions.
26979.m: At the Zibelemärit you buy onions.

26980.q: In which month does the Zibelemärit take place?
26980.e: The Zibelemärit takes place every year at the end of November. By then it is often already cold in Bern.

26981.q: How are the onions at the Zibelemärit often artistically presented?
26981.e: Farmers plait the onions into long strings and wreaths. These onion plaits are very popular.
26981.m: At the Zibelemärit there are plaited strings of onions.

26982.q: What do children like to throw at each other at the Zibelemärit?
26982.e: At the Zibelemärit children and teenagers throw confetti. Some also tap people with little plastic hammers.
26982.m: Lots of confetti flies at the Zibelemärit.

26983.q: Which baked dish with onions do people eat at the Zibelemärit?
26983.e: At the Zibelemärit many stalls sell warm onion tart. It is as much a part of the market as the onion plaits.
26983.m: At the Zibelemärit people eat onion tart.

26984.q: On which day of the week does the Zibelemärit take place?
26984.e: The Zibelemärit is always on the fourth Monday in November. Many people in Bern take the day off for it.
26984.m: The Zibelemärit is on a Monday.

27478.q: Which city did King Hammurabi rule over?
27478.e: Hammurabi (also Hammurapi) was king of Babylon. He made the city the centre of a large empire in Mesopotamia.
27478.m: Hammurabi was a powerful king of Babylon.

27479.q: In which script is the Code of Hammurabi written?
27479.e: In Mesopotamia people wrote with wedge-shaped signs. Hammurabi’s laws are also carved into the stone in cuneiform.
27479.m: The Code of Hammurabi is written in cuneiform.

27480.q: What did Hammurabi have his laws written on so that everyone could see them?
27480.e: The laws are on a stele over two metres high made of hard, dark stone. That way they were preserved for a long time.
27480.m: Hammurabi’s laws are on a stone pillar.

27481.q: What does the old rule “An eye for an eye, a tooth for a tooth” mean?
a: The punishment should match the harm
You should forgive everyone at once
Punishments are only paid in money
27481.e: Anyone who harmed someone was to suffer something equal. This principle is called the law of retaliation.
27481.m: “An eye for an eye” means the punishment matches the harm.

27482.q: According to the preface of his laws, whom did Hammurabi want to protect?
27482.e: In the prologue Hammurabi writes that he was to bring justice so that the strong would not harm the weak. In this way he presents himself as a just shepherd of his people.
27482.m: Hammurabi’s laws were meant to protect the weak from the strong.

27483.q: What did the size of a punishment in the Code of Hammurabi often depend on?
a: The social rank of offender and victim
The weather on the day of the crime
27483.e: Society was divided into free people, semi-free people and slaves. Anyone who injured a free person was usually punished more harshly than for injuring a slave.
27483.m: In the Code of Hammurabi the punishment often depended on the rank of those involved.

27484.q: In which present-day country was Hammurabi’s law stele rediscovered in 1901?
27484.e: An Elamite king had taken the stele to the city of Susa as war booty. There, in present-day Iran, French archaeologists found it again.
27484.m: Hammurabi’s stele was found in present-day Iran.

27485.q: According to the Code of Hammurabi, what punishment did a builder face if a house he built collapsed and killed the owner?
27485.e: The Code states that in this case the builder is to be put to death. The harsh rule was meant to make sure buildings were built carefully.
27485.m: The Code of Hammurabi punished bad builders very harshly.

27486.q: According to the epic, how much of Gilgamesh is divine?
27486.e: The epic describes Gilgamesh as two thirds god and one third human. His mother was the goddess Ninsun.
27486.m: According to the epic, Gilgamesh is two thirds divine.

27487.q: In which region is the Epic of Gilgamesh set?
27487.e: Gilgamesh was king of Uruk in southern Mesopotamia, in present-day Iraq. The oldest stories about him were written down in Sumerian.
27487.m: The Epic of Gilgamesh comes from Mesopotamia.

27488.q: Which goddess does Gilgamesh turn down when she wants to marry him?
27488.e: Gilgamesh lists how badly things went for her earlier lovers. Offended, the goddess then sends a monster against him.
27488.m: In the epic Gilgamesh rejects the goddess Ishtar.

27489.q: Which story from the Bible is the flood story in the Epic of Gilgamesh similar to?
27489.e: In the Epic of Gilgamesh, too, a man builds a boat and survives a great flood. In 1872 a researcher recognised this similarity on a clay tablet.
27489.m: The flood in the Epic of Gilgamesh is similar to the story of Noah.

27490.q: What is the Epic of Gilgamesh?
a: One of the oldest hero stories
27490.e: The Epic of Gilgamesh tells of King Gilgamesh and his search for immortality. The best-known version is on twelve clay tablets.
27490.m: The Epic of Gilgamesh is one of the oldest hero stories in the world.

27491.q: Roughly how old is the Epic of Gilgamesh?
27491.e: The first Gilgamesh stories were created about 4000 years ago. The best-known tablets come from the library of the Assyrian king Ashurbanipal in the 7th century BC.
27491.m: The Epic of Gilgamesh is several thousand years old.

27492.q: Which test does Gilgamesh fail at the home of the flood survivor?
27492.e: Gilgamesh is meant to show that he can conquer sleep. But he falls asleep at once and so proves that he cannot become immortal.
27492.m: Gilgamesh fails the test of staying awake.

27493.q: At the end of the epic, what does Gilgamesh proudly show on his return?
27493.e: At the end Gilgamesh takes his companion up onto the mighty wall of his city. His building thus becomes what remains of him.
27493.m: At the end of the epic Gilgamesh proudly shows the wall of his city.

27494.e: A ziggurat is a large tower made of several steps, with a shrine at the top. There were such buildings in many cities of Mesopotamia.
27494.m: A ziggurat is a stepped temple tower in Mesopotamia.

27495.q: Roughly how old is the Ziggurat of Ur?
27495.e: King Ur-Nammu had the ziggurat built around 2100 BC. That is about 4100 years ago.
27495.m: The Ziggurat of Ur is about 4000 years old.

27496.q: What happened to the Ziggurat of Ur about 1500 years after it was built?
a: A Babylonian king had it restored
It was turned into a church
It was excavated for the first time
27496.e: In the 6th century BC the Babylonian king Nabonidus had old shrines restored. These included the Ziggurat of Ur.
27496.m: The Ziggurat of Ur was already restored in ancient times.

27497.q: What is the core of the Ziggurat of Ur made of?
27497.e: In Mesopotamia there was hardly any stone, but lots of mud. The core is made of sun-dried bricks, the outer shell of fired bricks with bitumen as mortar.
27497.m: The Ziggurat of Ur was built of mud bricks.

27498.q: How did people get up the Ziggurat of Ur?
27498.e: At the front three staircases lead up, one straight from the front and two at the sides along the wall. They meet at the top at a gatehouse.
27498.m: Stairs on the outside led up the ziggurat.

27499.q: What did archaeologists find at Ur next to the ziggurat in the 1920s?
27499.e: The British archaeologist Leonard Woolley excavated Ur from 1922 to 1934. He found the ziggurat and tombs with gold, jewellery and musical instruments.
27499.m: Rich royal tombs were found at Ur.

27500.q: Which people made Ur one of their most important cities?
27500.e: Ur was one of the most important cities of the Sumerians in southern Mesopotamia. The Sumerians were one of the world’s first civilisations.
27500.m: Ur was an important city of the Sumerians.

27501.q: Which animals are shown on the bricks of the Ishtar Gate?
27501.e: Rows of bulls and dragons can be seen on the gate. They were sacred animals of the gods of Babylon.
27501.m: The Ishtar Gate shows bulls and dragons.

27502.q: In which city did the Ishtar Gate originally stand?
27502.e: The gate was one of the main gates in the city wall of Babylon. Through this gate you entered the inner city from the north.
27502.m: The Ishtar Gate was a city gate of Babylon.

27503.q: What was the goddess Ishtar, after whom the gate is named, responsible for?
27503.e: Ishtar was one of the most important goddesses of Mesopotamia. She was seen as the goddess of love, but also of war.
27503.m: Ishtar was the goddess of love and war.

27504.q: What is the main colour of the glazed bricks of the Ishtar Gate?
27504.e: The bricks are covered with a bright blue glaze. The yellow and brown animal figures stand out clearly against it.

27505.q: In which city is part of the Ishtar Gate in a museum today?
27505.e: German archaeologists took bricks from the gate to Berlin. In the Pergamon Museum the smaller front gate was rebuilt.
27505.m: The Ishtar Gate is now in Berlin.

27506.q: At which festival did the Babylonians march in a great procession through the Ishtar Gate?
27506.e: At the New Year festival, called Akitu, statues of the gods were carried through the gate in a solemn procession. The festival lasted several days in spring.
27506.m: At the New Year festival a procession passed through the Ishtar Gate.

27507.q: Roughly how old is the Ishtar Gate?
27507.e: The gate was built in Babylon around 575 BC. So it is about 2600 years old.
27507.m: The Ishtar Gate is about 2600 years old.

27508.q: On which river was the heartland of the Assyrians?
27508.e: The most important Assyrian cities lay on the upper Tigris in northern Mesopotamia. Today the area is part of northern Iraq.
27508.m: The heartland of the Assyrians was on the Tigris.

27509.q: What was the first capital of the Assyrians called, which has the same name as their chief god?
27509.e: The city of Assur was the religious centre of the Assyrians. The name of the people also comes from it and from the god of the same name.
27509.m: The city of Assur gave the Assyrians their name.

27510.q: Which huge stone figures guarded the gates of Assyrian palaces?
27510.e: The Assyrians called these guardian figures lamassu. They have the body of a bull or lion, wings and a bearded human head.
27510.m: Winged bulls with human heads guarded Assyrian gates.

27511.q: What did the Assyrians often do with conquered peoples to prevent uprisings?
a: They made them citizens of Assur.
They chose a new king for them.
27511.e: The Assyrians deported whole groups of people to other parts of their empire. People uprooted like this were meant to put up less resistance.
27511.m: The Assyrians often forcibly resettled conquered peoples.

27512.q: Which famous city on the Tigris was the Assyrian capital for a long time?
27512.e: Nineveh lay on the River Tigris in present-day Iraq. Under King Sennacherib it became the splendid capital of the Assyrian Empire.
27512.m: Nineveh was a great capital of the Assyrians.

27513.q: In which present-day country was the heartland of the Assyrians?
27513.e: The heartland of the Assyrians lay on the Tigris in the north of present-day Iraq. From there they conquered a large empire.
27513.m: The Assyrian Empire was centred in present-day Iraq.

27514.q: What did the Assyrian kings decorate the walls of their palaces with?
a: Stone reliefs of hunts and wars
27514.e: Large stone slabs with reliefs hung in the palaces. They showed the king hunting lions and his victories in war.
27514.m: Assyrian palaces were decorated with stone reliefs.

27515.q: Which country on the Nile did the Assyrians conquer in the 7th century BC?
27515.e: In 671 BC King Esarhaddon conquered Lower Egypt with the city of Memphis. With this, the Assyrian Empire reached its greatest size.
27515.m: In the 7th century BC the Assyrians even conquered Egypt.

27516.q: In which present-day country are the ruins of Nineveh?
27516.e: Nineveh lies on the Tigris near the present-day city of Mosul in northern Iraq.
27516.m: The ruins of Nineveh are in Iraq.

27517.q: Which people made Nineveh their capital?
27517.e: Around 700 BC the Assyrian king Sennacherib built Nineveh up splendidly. It became one of the largest cities of its time.
27517.m: Nineveh was the capital of the Assyrians.

27518.q: What happened to the Assyrian Empire after Nineveh was destroyed?
27518.e: Nineveh fell in 612 BC after a long siege. After that the Assyrian Empire collapsed within a few years.
27518.m: After the fall of Nineveh the Assyrian Empire fell apart.

27519.e: The Babylonian king Nabopolassar formed an alliance with the Medes from Iran. Together they defeated the Assyrians.
27519.m: Babylonians and Medes conquered Nineveh together.

27520.q: According to the Bible, which prophet was sent to Nineveh?
27520.e: In the Book of Jonah the prophet is meant to call on the people of Nineveh to change their ways. The story is well known because on the way Jonah is swallowed by a great fish.
27520.m: According to the Bible, the prophet Jonah was sent to Nineveh.

27521.q: What were the walls of the royal palaces in Nineveh decorated with?
27521.e: Stone reliefs showed the kings’ military campaigns, hunts and building works. In Sennacherib’s palace alone they were about three kilometres long.
27521.m: The palaces of Nineveh were decorated with stone reliefs.

27522.q: When was Nineveh excavated by researchers?
27522.e: The Briton Austen Henry Layard dug at Nineveh in the 1840s. Many finds went to the British Museum in London.
27522.m: Nineveh was excavated in the 19th century.

27523.q: In which city are the Hanging Gardens said to have stood?
27523.e: Ancient writers report that King Nebuchadnezzar II had the gardens made in Babylon. They have still not been found today.
27523.m: The Hanging Gardens are said to have stood in Babylon.

27524.q: Why do some researchers doubt that the Hanging Gardens in Babylon really existed?
a: No clear traces have been found
The gardens are said to have been made of gold
27524.e: No certain remains of the gardens have been found in Babylon. Herodotus, who described the city in detail, does not mention them either.
27524.m: Whether the Hanging Gardens existed is uncertain.

27525.q: According to tradition, for whom did the king of Babylon build the Hanging Gardens?
a: For his wife, who was homesick for her mountains
For his soldiers after a victory
For the gods of the sea
27525.e: Queen Amytis came from a mountainous land. In flat Babylon she is said to have been homesick. The green terraces were meant to remind her of her home.
27525.m: The gardens are said to have been built for a homesick queen.

27526.q: Which other building, like the Hanging Gardens, is one of the Seven Wonders of the Ancient World?
27526.e: The Seven Wonders of the Ancient World include the Pyramids of Giza and the Hanging Gardens. The pyramids are the only one still standing.
27526.m: The Hanging Gardens are one of the Seven Wonders of the Ancient World.

27527.q: Why are the gardens of Babylon called “hanging”?
a: The plants grew on high terraces and hung down
They were on a cliff above the sea
27527.e: The gardens are said to have been laid out on terraces one above the other. From below it looked as if the plants were hanging over the walls.
27527.m: The Hanging Gardens were on high terraces.

27528.q: In which present-day country are the ruins of Babylon, where people search for the gardens?
27528.e: Babylon lies about 90 kilometres south of Baghdad. Since 2019 the ruins have been a UNESCO World Heritage Site.
27528.m: The ruins of Babylon are in present-day Iraq.

27529.q: From which river would water have had to be lifted for the gardens in Babylon?
27529.e: Babylon lay on the Euphrates. For plants on high terraces, water would have had to be raised with lifting machines.
27529.m: Babylon lay on the River Euphrates.

27530.q: In which region was the Hittite Empire?
27530.e: The Hittite Empire lay in the centre of Anatolia, in present-day Turkey. Later its influence reached as far as Syria.
27530.m: The Hittites lived in Anatolia in present-day Turkey.

27531.q: With which mighty empire on the Nile did the Hittites make a famous peace treaty?
27531.e: After long fighting, the Hittite king and Pharaoh Ramesses II made peace. The treaty is seen as one of the oldest peace treaties that has come down to us.
27531.m: The Hittites made peace with Egypt.

27532.q: Which gate with two stone beasts of prey is a landmark of Hattusa?
27532.e: At the Lion Gate, two lions carved from the stone stand guard. It was an entrance in the wall of the upper city.
27532.m: The Lion Gate is a landmark of the Hittite capital.

27533.q: Where does a copy of the peace treaty between the Hittites and the Egyptians hang?
a: At the UN headquarters in New York
In the Federal Palace in Bern
In the White House in Washington
27533.e: The treaty between King Hattusili III and Pharaoh Ramesses II is seen as one of the oldest peace treaties that has come down to us. That is why a copy of the clay tablet hangs at the United Nations.
27533.m: A copy of the Hittite-Egyptian peace treaty hangs at the UN.

27535.q: What did researchers find in large numbers in the Hittite capital?
27535.e: Thousands of clay tablets were found in Hattusa. Since the Hittite language was deciphered in 1915, they can be read and tell us a lot about the Hittites.
27535.m: Clay tablets reveal a lot about the Hittites.

27536.q: Which weapon made the Hittites especially feared?
27536.e: The Hittites used horse-drawn chariots with a crew of three. With them they could attack quickly and with great force.
27536.m: The Hittites were feared for their chariots.

27537.q: Roughly when did the Hittite Empire fall apart?
27537.e: Around 1200 BC several empires in the eastern Mediterranean collapsed. Hattusa too was abandoned at this time.
27537.m: The Hittite Empire fell apart around 1200 BC.

27538.q: Which empire did Nebuchadnezzar II rule?
27538.e: Nebuchadnezzar II was the most important king of the Neo-Babylonian Empire. Under him Babylon reached its greatest splendour.
27538.m: Nebuchadnezzar II was king of the Neo-Babylonian Empire.

27539.q: Roughly when did Nebuchadnezzar II rule?
27539.e: He ruled from 605 to 562 BC, so for over 40 years. That is about 1100 years after Hammurabi.

27540.q: Which city did Nebuchadnezzar II conquer in 587/586 BC, destroying its temple?
27540.e: After an uprising his army besieged the city and destroyed the temple. After that the kingdom lost its independence.
27540.m: Nebuchadnezzar II destroyed the temple in Jerusalem in 587/586 BC.

27541.q: Which army did Nebuchadnezzar defeat as crown prince in 605 BC?
a: The army of the Germanic peoples
27541.e: At the Battle of Carchemish on the Euphrates he beat the pharaoh’s army. After that Babylon was the leading power in the region.
27541.m: Nebuchadnezzar defeated the Egyptians in 605 BC.

27542.q: Which wonder of the world is often linked with Nebuchadnezzar and Babylon?
27542.e: According to a legend, Nebuchadnezzar had the Hanging Gardens made for his wife. Whether they really existed is still disputed today.
27542.m: The Hanging Gardens are seen as Babylon’s wonder of the world.

27543.q: What did Nebuchadnezzar have built in Babylon for the city god Marduk?
27543.e: Marduk was the chief god of Babylon. Nebuchadnezzar had his temple, the Esagila, and the stepped tower next to it splendidly enlarged.
27543.m: Nebuchadnezzar built great temples for Marduk.

27544.q: In which book of the Bible does a prophet interpret Nebuchadnezzar’s dreams?
27544.e: In the Book of Daniel the king dreams, among other things, of a great statue made of different metals. Daniel interprets this dream for him.
27544.m: In the Book of Daniel the prophet interprets Nebuchadnezzar’s dreams.

27545.q: Which opera by Giuseppe Verdi is named after Nebuchadnezzar?
27545.e: “Nabucco” is the short Italian form of Nebuchadnezzar. The Chorus of the Hebrew Slaves from it is especially famous.

27546.q: Which great empire did Cyrus the Great found?
27546.e: Cyrus II is seen as the founder of the first great Persian empire. It later stretched from Egypt to India.
27546.m: Cyrus the Great founded the Persian Empire.

27547.q: According to tradition, how did Cyrus often treat conquered peoples?
a: He let them keep their religion and customs
He forced everyone to speak Persian
27547.e: Cyrus was seen as a mild ruler. He often let peoples worship their gods and keep their customs.
27547.m: Cyrus let conquered peoples keep their religion.

27548.q: Which king of Lydia, famous for being rich, did Cyrus defeat?
27548.e: Croesus ruled in Sardis in Lydia and was famous for his wealth. That is why people still say “as rich as Croesus” today.
27548.m: Cyrus defeated the rich Lydian king Croesus.

27549.q: Which famous city did Cyrus conquer in 539 BC?
27549.e: Cyrus entered Babylon in 539 BC. After that the whole of Mesopotamia belonged to the Persian Empire.

27550.q: According to the Bible, what did Cyrus allow the Judeans who had been taken to Babylon to do?
a: Build a city on the Nile
27550.e: According to the Book of Ezra, they were allowed to return and rebuild their temple. That is why Cyrus is shown very positively in the Bible.
27550.m: Cyrus allowed the deported Judeans to return home.

27551.q: In which present-day country is the tomb of Cyrus the Great?
27551.e: The simple stone tomb stands in Pasargadae, the first capital of the Persian Empire, in present-day Iran.
27551.m: The tomb of Cyrus is in present-day Iran.

27552.q: How large did the Persian Empire become under Cyrus and his successors?
a: It stretched from Egypt to India
It reached as far as America
27552.e: Cyrus conquered large areas, his successors even more. The Persian Empire was then the largest empire in the world.
27552.m: The Persian Empire stretched from Egypt to India.

27553.q: According to the historian Herodotus, how did Cyrus the Great die?
27553.e: According to Herodotus, Cyrus fell in 530 BC fighting the Massagetae, a people of horsemen in Central Asia.
27553.m: According to Herodotus, Cyrus fell fighting a people of horsemen.

27554.q: How did Darius I govern his huge Persian Empire?
a: He divided it into provinces with governors
He let all the cities vote for themselves
He left it to the priests
27554.e: Darius divided the empire into provinces called satrapies. Each was run by a governor and had to pay taxes to the king.
27554.m: Darius I divided the Persian Empire into provinces.

27555.q: Which empire did King Darius I rule?
27555.e: Darius I ruled the Persian Empire from 522 to 486 BC. It stretched from Egypt to India.
27555.m: Darius I was king of the Persian Empire.

27557.q: What did Darius I introduce to make trade easier in his empire?
27557.e: Darius had a gold coin minted that is called the daric after him. It was valid throughout the empire.
27557.m: Darius I introduced a standard gold coin.

27559.q: What was there at regular intervals along the Persian Royal Road?
27559.e: There were over 100 stations along the road. There, messengers could change horses and ride on quickly.
27559.m: On the Royal Road messengers changed horses at stations.

27560.q: Through which great empire did the Persian Royal Road run?
27560.e: The road linked important cities of the Persian Empire, from present-day Iran to Asia Minor in present-day Turkey.
27560.m: The Royal Road crossed the Persian Empire.

27561.q: Which canal did Darius I have completed in Egypt?
a: A canal from the Nile to the Red Sea
A canal from the Nile to the Euphrates
A canal through the Isthmus of Corinth
A canal to the Dead Sea
27561.e: The canal linked the Nile with the Red Sea and so the Mediterranean with the Indian Ocean. Darius had inscriptions put up to commemorate its construction.
27561.m: Darius I had a canal from the Nile to the Red Sea completed.

27562.q: What did the Persian kings mainly use Persepolis for?
a: As a splendid residence for festivals and receptions
As a harbour for the war fleet
27562.e: The Persian kings had palaces and halls built in Persepolis. There they received envoys and held great festivals.
27562.m: Persepolis was a splendid residence of the Persian kings.

27563.q: Who had Persepolis set on fire in 330 BC?
27563.e: After his victory over the Persians, Alexander captured the city. Afterwards the palaces burnt down, perhaps as revenge for the destruction of Athens by the Persians.
27563.m: Alexander the Great had Persepolis burnt down in 330 BC.

27564.q: In which present-day country are the ruins of Persepolis?
27564.e: Persepolis lies in south-west Iran, north-east of the city of Shiraz. The ruins are among the best-known sights in the country.
27564.m: The ruins of Persepolis are in Iran.

27565.q: What held up the roof of the great audience hall in Persepolis?
27565.e: The roof of the audience hall rested on 72 columns that were about 20 metres high. Some of them still stand today.
27565.m: The audience hall in Persepolis was a huge hall of columns.

27566.q: What do the famous reliefs on the staircases of Persepolis show?
a: Delegations bringing gifts to the king
27566.e: The reliefs show delegations from many peoples of the empire with gifts such as animals, fabrics and vessels. This shows how large the empire was.
27566.m: The staircase reliefs of Persepolis show gift bearers from many peoples.

27567.q: What can still be seen of Persepolis today?
a: Ruins with columns, stairs and reliefs
Just a hole in the ground
27567.e: The palaces burnt down over 2000 years ago. Columns, stairs, gates and many reliefs have survived. The ruins are a UNESCO World Heritage Site.
27567.m: The ruins of Persepolis are a UNESCO World Heritage Site.

27568.q: What does the Greek name “Persepolis” mean?
27568.e: The Greek word “polis” means city. The Persians themselves called the place Parsa.
27568.m: Persepolis means city of the Persians.

27569.q: Where does the word “Samaritan”, used for people who help others, come from?
a: From the region of Samaria in ancient Israel
27569.e: Samaria was the capital and region of the northern kingdom of Israel. In the Bible a “Good Samaritan” helps an injured man, hence the name for helpers.
27569.m: Samaritans are named after the region of Samaria.

27570.q: What happened to many people of the northern kingdom of Israel after it was conquered?
27570.e: The Assyrians conquered the northern kingdom in 722 BC. Part of the population was taken to other areas of the empire.
27570.m: After the conquest many people from Israel were deported.

27571.q: According to the Bible, after the death of which king did the kingdom split into Israel and Judah?
27571.e: According to the Bible, the northern tribes refused to accept Solomon’s son as king. So around 926 BC a northern kingdom and a southern kingdom came into being.
27571.m: According to the Bible, the kingdom split after Solomon’s death.

27572.q: According to the Bible, how many tribes belonged to the northern kingdom of Israel?
27572.e: According to the Bible, ten of the twelve tribes of Israel formed the northern kingdom. Because they disappeared after the conquest, people speak of the “lost tribes”.
27572.m: According to the Bible, ten tribes belonged to the northern kingdom of Israel.

27573.q: What was the capital of the Kingdom of Judah?
27573.e: Jerusalem was the seat of the kings and of the temple. Judah was the smaller southern kingdom.
27573.m: Jerusalem was the capital of the Kingdom of Judah.

27574.q: What is the period called when many Judeans were taken to Babylon?
27574.e: After the fall of Jerusalem, part of Judah’s upper class lived in Babylonia for decades. This period had a strong influence on the Jewish religion.
27574.m: The deportation of the Judeans to Babylon is called the Babylonian Exile.

27575.q: According to the Bible, which family did the kings of Judah come from?
27575.e: According to the Bible, descendants of David ruled in Judah until the end of the kingdom. An inscription from Tel Dan also mentions a “House of David”.
27575.m: The kings of Judah were seen as descendants of David.

27576.q: What did King Hezekiah have built in Jerusalem around 700 BC to supply the city during a siege?
27576.e: The Siloam Tunnel is over 500 metres long and carried spring water into the city. So the people had water even during a siege.
27576.m: King Hezekiah had a water tunnel built in Jerusalem.

27577.q: Which word for people comes from the name Judah?
27577.e: The name of the tribe and Kingdom of Judah became the name for the whole people. The English word “Jews” comes from it.
27577.m: The word “Jews” comes from the name Judah.

27578.q: In which period were the great Pyramids of Giza built?
27578.e: The Pyramids of Giza were built around 2600 to 2500 BC under pharaohs of the 4th Dynasty. This time belongs to the Old Kingdom.
27578.m: The Pyramids of Giza date from the Old Kingdom.

27579.q: Into how many great kingdoms is the history of ancient Egypt usually divided?
27579.e: People distinguish the Old, the Middle and the New Kingdom. In between there were unsettled times when the country fell apart.
27579.m: Ancient Egypt had an Old, a Middle and a New Kingdom.

27580.q: Which crown did the pharaoh wear after Upper and Lower Egypt were united?
27580.e: Upper Egypt had a white crown, Lower Egypt a red one. The pharaoh of the united country wore both together as a double crown.
27580.m: The double crown showed that the pharaoh ruled all of Egypt.

27581.q: Which weapon of war did the Egyptians only learn about from foreigners from western Asia?
27581.e: Foreign rulers from western Asia brought horses and chariots to Egypt. After that the pharaohs also used chariots in war.
27581.m: Foreigners from western Asia brought the chariot to Egypt.

27582.q: Which city was the most important religious centre of Egypt in the New Kingdom?
27582.e: Thebes, today’s Luxor, was the city of the god Amun. Huge temples were built there, and the royal tombs on the west bank.
27582.m: Thebes was the religious heart of Egypt in the New Kingdom.

27583.q: What do you call a series of rulers who come from the same family?
27583.e: The pharaohs are divided into dynasties. Often a son followed his father onto the throne.
27583.m: Rulers from the same family form a dynasty.

27584.q: After the death of which ruler did the Ptolemaic period begin in Egypt?
27584.e: Alexander the Great conquered Egypt in 332 BC. After his death his general Ptolemy took over the country and founded his own dynasty.
27584.m: The Ptolemies followed Alexander the Great.

27585.q: Which part of the country is called Lower Egypt?
a: The Nile Delta in the north
The Nile Valley in the south
27585.e: The Nile flows from south to north. That is why the area downstream, the delta on the Mediterranean, is called Lower Egypt.
27585.m: Lower Egypt is the Nile Delta in the north.

a: She was a woman who ruled as pharaoh
She was the first queen of Rome
27586.e: Hatshepsut had herself crowned pharaoh and ruled for about 20 years. Women on the pharaoh’s throne were very rare.
